title: Preregistered Paired Evaluation of a Deterministic Verifier Pipeline for LLM‑Generated Network Configuration Changes — Non‑informative Result under Shared‑Generation Semantics
abstract: We report a fully preregistered, archived paired experiment (cand‑2026‑01‑prereg‑v1) that tested whether deterministic tool‑augmentation (generate → deterministic validator → optional repair) reduces verifier‑detected unsafe intent→configuration proposals from a hosted LLM on synthetic NetOps tasks. Design: N=200 unique intent→configuration tasks in a paired design comparing (a) baseline LLM‑only and (b) guarded pipeline (gpt‑5‑mini + deterministic_netops_validator_v5). The run used shared_initial_candidate generation semantics (one LLM call per task) producing model_calls_used = 200 (preregistered independent per‑arm generation would have used up to 400). Observed (adversarial cluster): baseline SAFE = 200/200; guarded SAFE = 200/200 (paired contingency n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0). Estimate of paired SAFE‑rate difference = 0.0; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (resamples = 10000, seed = 1729). Because identical per‑pair generations were produced and the observed baseline unsafe rate was 0%, the preregistered causal hypothesis (that the deterministic verifier reduces unsafe proposals) was not testable in this execution. We publish the complete preregistered run and artifacts, offer an artifact‑grounded diagnosis of why the confirmatory test was non‑informative, and give concrete, artifact‑supported recommendations (independent per‑arm generation budgeting, adversarial calibration using the reserved exploratory budget, and deterministic pilot checks) to enable informative repeats.

sections.introduction:
Automating natural‑language intent → device‑configuration translation with large language models (LLMs) promises operational efficiency in NetOps but risks outages and policy violations when generated sequences violate ordering, dependency, or policy constraints. A widely proposed mitigation is tool‑augmentation: couple LLMs with deterministic validators/simulators in generate–validate–(repair) loops so that produced configurations are checked before execution. Prior work documents both promise and sensitivity to evaluation semantics: gains from tool‑augmentation are task‑dependent and can hinge on verifier fidelity, sampling semantics, and repair policies [1,2,3].

Motivated by a literature gap—few reproducible, preregistered adversarial NetOps experiments that measure the causal effect of adding deterministic validators—we preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory study (cand‑2026‑01‑prereg‑v1). The primary estimand was the paired SAFE‑rate difference (guarded − baseline) tested with an exact McNemar two‑sided test and paired bootstrap CI. Our contribution is empirical and methodological: we (1) release a fully archived preregistered paired run comparing a hosted LLM (gpt‑5‑mini) against a validator‑augmented pipeline; (2) analyze, using archived artifacts, why the confirmatory contrast was uninformative under the executed semantics; and (3) provide reproducible design recommendations to make future repeats informative under the same preregistration framework.
sections.related_work:
Surveys and prototype reports document rapid adoption of LLMs in NetOps tasks (intent translation, configuration synthesis, remediation) while calling for workflow‑centred, sandboxed evaluations that capture stateful, multi‑device risk [4,5]. Empirical and method papers show that generate–validate–refine and divide–verify–refine pipelines can reduce constraint violations on curated tasks if the external verifier faithfully encodes domain constraints, but reported effects vary with sampling and repair policies [2,6].

Red‑teaming and guardrail studies in adjacent domains emphasize adversarial calibration and ROC‑style diagnostics (false negatives vs false refusals) as necessary complements to single‑arm correctness measures [3,7]. Evaluation methodology work for agentic NetOps recommends deterministic task generators, explicit initial/final states, and archived validator traces to enable replayable, auditable experiments [5]. Our study follows these methodological prescriptions: deterministic task generation, preregistered paired estimand, sandboxed deterministic validation, and full archival of execution and analysis artifacts to permit deterministic replay and diagnosis.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand. The experiment was preregistered (cand‑2026‑01‑prereg‑v1). Primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (guarded − baseline) on binary SAFE indicators produced by a deterministic sandbox validator. Confirmatory test: exact two‑sided McNemar; CI: paired bootstrap percentile (10000 resamples, seed = 1729). Planned N=200 paired tasks (400 episodes) was chosen to detect an ≈7 percentage‑point paired reduction under assumed baseline unsafe rate ≈10–15% (power ≈80%).

Task generation and scope. A deterministic generator produced 200 synthetic intent→configuration tasks restricted to IPv4 reachability and simple device fields (admin, mtu, vlan) across single‑AS, multi‑device topologies. Each task manifest included initial_state, expected_final_state, required_sequence, and difficulty metadata. Tasks were partitioned into benign and adversarial prompt transforms per a preregistered obfuscation rule set; a preregistered exploratory reserve (up to 50 tasks) was retained for ROC/refusal calibration.

Pipelines and generation semantics. Baseline: post‑hoc scoring of an LLM candidate with deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (no runtime enforcement). Guarded: deterministic validation of candidate in a sandbox; repairs were permitted by design but none were invoked in confirmatory episodes. The preregistration allowed two generation semantics: (A) independent per‑arm generation (one LLM call per arm per task; ~400 model calls) or (B) shared_initial_candidate (single LLM call per task shared across arms; ~200 calls). The executed run used the shared_initial_candidate semantics to conserve model budget; model_calls_used = 200 (manifested in the execution manifest).

Scoring, exclusions, and analysis. The validator produced deterministic valid flags and violation lists; confirmatory binary outcome = validator.valid (1 = SAFE, 0 = UNSAFE). Preregistered exclusion rules (duplicates, verifier nondeterminism) and retry policy (one retry on model error) were enforced automatically. The analysis executor (paired_binary_analysis_v1) computed contingency counts n11,n10,n01,n00, exact McNemar p, and paired bootstrap CIs (10000 resamples, seed = 1729). Deterministic reconciliation and provider audit checks ensured no technical failures occurred in the confirmatory run.
sections.results:
Execution accounting. The preregistered paired design yielded completed_episode_count = 400 (200 paired episodes), failed_episode_count = 0, and model_calls_used = 200 under shared_initial_candidate semantics (preregistered independent per‑arm generation would have required up to 400 calls). No exclusions, replacements, or nondeterministic validator behaviors occurred; deterministic reconciliation checks passed.

Primary outcomes. The deterministic validator labeled every confirmatory candidate SAFE: baseline SAFE = 200/200 and guarded SAFE = 200/200. Contingency counts: n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Paired SAFE‑rate difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (resamples = 10000, bootstrap_seed = 1729). These numbers are the direct archived outputs of the preregistered analysis executor and appear unchanged in the analysis artifacts.

Diagnostic traces. Representative scoring JSONs show identical generated candidates for baseline and guarded episodes and validator traces with violation_count = 0 and repair_provider_trace = null. Because the guarded arm performed only validation (no repairs applied) and both arms scored the same candidate, no discordant paired outcomes could arise. The observed ceiling outcome therefore reflects the executed sampling semantics combined with the sampled model behavior rather than evidence that the validator is unnecessary in general.

Exploratory reserves. The preregistered exploratory budget reserved up to 50 tasks for ROC/refusal calibration; that reserve was not consumed before confirmatory execution and thus no ROC or refusal‑rate estimates were produced in this run.
sections.discussion:
Interpretation of the degenerate contingency. McNemar’s test requires discordant pairs (n10 or n01) to detect paired differences; their absence yields a degenerate p = 1.0 and CI at zero. In our execution the degenerate contingency followed from three archived facts: (1) shared_initial_candidate semantics (one LLM call per task shared across arms), (2) validator.valid = true for every sampled candidate, and (3) no repairs were applied in confirmatory episodes. The conjunction of these facts made the preregistered causal contrast mechanically untestable.

Design lessons and artifact‑grounded recommendations. All recommendations follow directly from the preregistration and execution artifacts:
- Use independent per‑arm generation when testing a validator’s causal effect via paired contrasts unless the guarded arm will deterministically alter candidates (repairs) at run time. Independent draws enable arm‑level stochasticity and require additional model calls (≈+200 calls for N=200 in our setting).
- Before running confirmatory episodes, consume the preregistered exploratory reserve to calibrate adversarial transforms until the baseline unsafe rate aligns with power assumptions; archive the calibration and freeze parameters so the confirmatory assumptions remain preregistered.
- Include a deterministic pilot check on a small holdout to detect ceiling/floor contingencies; if the pilot produces no discordant pairs, follow preregistered contingency‑preserving adaptations (e.g., enable independent draws or strengthen adversarial transforms) rather than proceeding with an uninformative test.
- If repairs are part of the guarded pipeline, ensure repair_provider_trace artifacts are captured and analyzed to quantify UNSAFE→SAFE conversions and any repair‑induced regressions. In this run repair traces are null, so repairs were not a mechanism for inducing discordance.

Alternative estimands under budget constraints. When per‑arm independence is infeasible, consider alternative preregistered estimands that remain testable under shared generation: absolute baseline unsafe‑rate estimation with CIs, guarded pipeline refusal and post‑repair SAFE rates, or exploratory ROC estimation using injected ground‑truth unsafe examples. These alternatives change resource needs but preserve inferential validity; they are anticipated by secondary_estimands in the preregistration.

Threats to validity and externality. Internal validity: the principal threat to the original inference here was generation semantics (shared vs independent) that eliminated arm‑level variation. Construct validity: the synthetic task family restricts fields and topologies; validator completeness relative to real‑world failure modes is limited. External validity: results from gpt‑5‑mini on our synthetic tasks do not generalize to multi‑vendor, multi‑AS production networks. Conclusion validity: the observed zero discordance invalidates the preregistered power calculation assumptions and therefore precludes inferential claims about validator effectiveness. These limitations are captured in the archived preregistration and execution artifacts and are summarized in the Limitations section below.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully archived preregistered paired experiment comparing gpt‑5‑mini baseline generation and a deterministic validator‑augmented pipeline on 200 synthetic NetOps tasks. Under executed shared_initial_candidate semantics both arms produced zero verifier‑detected unsafe proposals (paired difference = 0.0; exact McNemar p = 1.0; 95% CI = [0.0,0.0]). Because identical per‑pair generations were used and because the baseline unsafe rate was 0%, the preregistered causal hypothesis was not testable for this run. The scientific contribution is therefore methodological and reproducibility‑centred: (1) a complete deterministic preregistered run with archived artifacts that permit exact replay; (2) an artifact‑grounded diagnosis of why the execution was non‑informative for verifier efficacy; and (3) concrete, artifact‑supported recommendations (independent per‑arm generation budgeting, adversarial calibration with exploratory reserves, and pilot contingency checks) to enable informative repeats. Practitioners planning confirmatory paired designs should align generation semantics and resource budgeting with the estimand before execution and consume exploratory reserve for adversarial calibration to prevent ceiling/floor contingencies.

limitations: Synthetic tasks and scope: tasks were deterministic synthetic topologies produced by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 and limited to single‑AS, multi‑device setups; results may not generalize to production, multi‑AS, or vendor‑specific features.

Generation semantics: the executed run used shared_initial_candidate (independent_condition_generation = false), producing identical per‑pair generations and creating a ceiling effect when shared candidates were valid.

Adversarial strength: the preregistered adversarial templates used in this run did not elicit unsafe outputs from gpt‑5‑mini on the sampled tasks; stronger adversarial cases or explicit injected unsafe examples are required to measure verifier effect.
Single‑model scope: only the declared model (gpt‑5‑mini) was evaluated; no multi‑model generality is claimed.

Verifier completeness: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 ran deterministically in synthetic sandboxed states; external validation of validator completeness against all real‑world NetOps failure modes is not provided.

Operational external validity: no production deployment, operator‑in‑the‑loop workload measurement, nor multi‑vendor field trials were performed; operator‑cost trade‑offs remain unquantified at scale.
